results.summary: This design displays the letter P on a seven-segment display when a correct secret code is entered on the input switches. It is a first Tiny Tapeout chip built in Wokwi, with four input pins and four output pins. Testing is done by trying different DIP switch positions to find the code. The documentation deliberately withholds the code logic, so the exact behaviour cannot be verified from the text.

This project is described as a broken counter that turns on four outputs one after another with button presses and turns them off again with two presses. It uses a clock and a button input, and requires external hardware to generate current, a button, and something to display the outputs. The documentation is thin and the design is explicitly labelled broken, so its intended behaviour is unclear. Testing consists of pressing the button at least six times.

This design checks eight switches arranged in pairs and lights a seven-segment display with a zero only when exactly one pair is on. It uses logic gates to detect pairs and filter the result, with outputs on the bidirectional pins. Testing is done by manually flipping switches in the Wokwi online project, and the seven-segment display from the template is the only external hardware. The description notes the behaviour may change later.

This is a workshop experiment with randomly placed gates, including a flip-flop and a ring oscillator, that the author states does not do anything useful yet. It has a flip-flop input and output, a ring enable input, and a ring oscillator output. Testing is described as powering on and hoping for the best, with a microswitch for input and an oscilloscope for output. The documentation is minimal and the design is explicitly a non-functional experiment.

This project is a simple two-input logic block described as a complexer, with two inputs and three outputs. The documentation says only that inputs one and two control the outputs, without specifying the logic function. No external hardware is required. The description is too thin to determine what the circuit actually computes.

This design is a seven-segment decoder that takes seven switch inputs and drives seven segment outputs. Each switch is supposed to turn on another segment, according to the documentation. A seven-segment display is the only external hardware needed. The documentation is very brief and does not describe the decoding logic in detail.

This project is a first Wokwi design described as a logic circuit test for the Wokwi platform. It has eight input pins and eight output pins but the documentation does not explain what logic is implemented. Testing is described only as a test for Wokwi. The documentation is essentially a placeholder and gives no useful description of the design.

This design implements basic logic gates, with outputs labelled for AND, OR, NOT and NAND functions driven by eight inputs. Pressing buttons changes the lights according to the gate logic. The documentation is largely placeholder text with question marks, so the exact mapping of inputs to gates is unclear. No external hardware is specified.

This project implements a full adder and full subtractor with two 4-bit registers, selecting the operation and destination register via control inputs. Data is entered in binary on four input pins, the register is chosen with one input, and add or subtract is chosen with another. Outputs provide four data bits plus an overflow bit for subtraction. No external hardware is required, though LEDs and switches are suggested for convenience.

This design combines a mutex arbiter, an inefficient C-gate, and an LFSR that drives a 4-bit pseudo-random output. The mutex grant outputs and C-gate output are exposed alongside the LFSR bits for observation. Testing checks that mutex grants are mutually exclusive, that the C-gate behaves correctly, and that the LFSR produces a 4-bit PRNG sequence. The documentation does not specify any external hardware.
